summary:
1 and 2 Chronicles were a single book in Hebrew tradition; the Greek translators split it in two. It retells Israel's story for the community that had returned from exile — the deportation to Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC — and opens with nine chapters of genealogies, family-line lists running from Adam through the twelve tribes. The lists set the returned community inside one continuous story, record tribal lands, and preserve the service rosters of the priests and Levites (the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve Israel's sanctuary); chapter 9 brings them down to the families who resettled Jerusalem after the exile. Much of what follows is also told in Samuel and Kings, but the selection differs: Saul's reign takes one chapter (his death, chapter 10), David's failures with Bathsheba and Absalom are not retold, and the northern kingdom's kings appear only where they touch Judah.

The rest of the book is David. He takes Jerusalem and brings up the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the Law — a first attempt ends with Uzzah struck dead for touching it (chapter 13); it arrives when the Levites carry it as the Law prescribes (15:2), with singers and a psalm of thanksgiving (16). When David proposes to build God a house, God turns the offer around through the prophet Nathan: "the LORD will build a house for you" (17:10) — a dynasty. "He will build a house for Me, and I will establish his throne forever" (17:12); the New Testament opens by tracing Jesus to this line: "Jesus Christ, the son of David" (Matthew 1:1). A census David orders brings a plague that halts at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite; David buys the site and declares, "Here shall be the house of the LORD God" (22:1) — the spot where 2 Chronicles 3:1 places Solomon's temple.

David himself is not allowed to build it: "You are not to build a house for My Name, because you are a man of war who has shed blood" (28:3). So the closing chapters are preparation — stone, iron, cedar, and gold stockpiled, and rosters (chapters 23–27) assigning divisions of priests, Levites, musicians, and gatekeepers for a temple that does not yet exist. David commissions Solomon before all Israel, the leaders give freewill offerings, and David prays: "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty, for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You… For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You" (29:11, 14). The book ends with David dead "at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor" and Solomon on the throne (29:28).
